[1] The hospital hired me the June I turned sixteen, which was the youngest it hired anyone, and it put me in Patient Transport because Transport was where you could do the least harm. I was given a navy polo shirt with the department's name stitched over the pocket, a badge that opened four doors out of the building's several hundred, and a trainer named Mrs. Ferreira, who had been pushing wheelchairs and stretchers through St. Columba's for nineteen years and who looked at my new shoes on the first morning and said only, "You'll want a second pair."

[2] The job, as it was explained to me in orientation, was a matter of getting bodies from one place to another: from a ward to X-ray, from the emergency department to a bed upstairs, from a bed to the front door and a waiting car. Every request came through a pager clipped to my belt, and every request had a time on it. The dispatcher, a man I never once saw in person, kept a running count of how long each of us took from pickup to drop-off, and on Fridays the count was posted beside the time clock. I read that list the way I had read report cards. I meant to be near the top of it by August.

[3] Mrs. Ferreira was nowhere near the top of it. I noticed this in my first week and decided, with the confidence of someone who had worked there four days, that she was slow because she was old. She did not take the service elevators, which were fast and empty and smelled of floor wax; she took the public ones, which stopped on every floor. Going to Radiology from the fourth-floor wards, she did not cut through the loading corridor behind the kitchens, which saved three minutes; she went the long way, down the glass walkway that crossed above the parking garage, where the afternoon sun came in so hard you had to squint.

[4] I said something about it on the second Thursday. We were bringing a man named Mr. Adeyemi down for a scan, and he had been quiet the whole way, his hands flat on the blanket over his knees. When Mrs. Ferreira turned toward the walkway, I said, quietly I thought, that the corridor was quicker. She did not answer me. She slowed the chair, instead, at the middle of the glass, where you could see the whole lot and the road beyond it and a line of plane trees along the river, and Mr. Adeyemi lifted his head and looked for a long time at the trees. "Eleven days," he said, to no one exactly. Then she pushed on.

[5] I did not understand it then; at the time I filed it as one more thing she did instead of hurrying. What I did notice was that people asked for her. Nurses would page Transport and say that, if it was possible, they would like Mrs. Ferreira for this one, and the dispatcher, who cared about nothing but the count, would grumble and send her anyway. I assumed this was about seniority. It took me most of July to see that the patients they asked her for were the ones who had been upstairs the longest.

[6] In my last week she was out sick, and a request came through for a woman going home after a month on the cardiac floor. Her daughter was bringing the car around. The service elevator was standing open when I reached it, and I had the woman in the chair, and the loading corridor would have put us at the front entrance a good four minutes early, which would have looked fine on Friday's list. I stood there long enough that she asked if something was wrong.

[7] I said no. I took the public elevator, which stopped on three, and on two, and I took her down the glass walkway, and I did not stop in the middle, because I did not feel I had earned that; I only slowed. She did not say anything about the trees. She put her hand up against the glass, flat, the way you would touch the side of an animal to see if it would let you, and kept it there until we reached the far end.

[8] My time for that run was the worst I posted all summer. I remember being surprised that I did not mind, and then being surprised, years later, at how clearly I could still see her hand.

[1] Spend a morning in a room full of four-year-olds and you will hear a great deal of talk that is addressed to no one. A boy building a tower narrates the job as he goes ("the big one, no, the big one goes here") without looking up to see whether anyone is listening. A girl at a puzzle tells herself, in a fair imitation of her teacher's voice, to try the corners first. Adults tend to find this charming and assume it is a phase. On the second point they are right. On what kind of phase it is, two of the twentieth century's most influential students of childhood disagreed, and the disagreement turned out to be about more than talk.

[2] The Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget, recording the conversations of children at a school in Geneva in the 1920s, was struck by how much of what the youngest said made no attempt to reach a listener. He called it egocentric speech. The label was not meant as an insult. For Piaget, young children were egocentric in a technical sense: they had not yet learned to take another person's point of view, and their speech reflected that limitation. Talk of this kind, he thought, was thinking that had not yet been socialized. As children grew and learned to adapt their speech to others, it would fade, and by the early school years most of it would be gone. It was a symptom of immaturity, and it disappeared because the immaturity did.

[3] The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, writing in the following decade, accepted Piaget's observations and rejected his explanation. Vygotsky argued that a child's talk to herself was not a failed attempt at conversation but a successful use of language for a new purpose: guiding her own behavior. Speech begins, in his account, as something that passes between people, as when an adult tells a child what to do next. The child then turns that tool on herself, saying aloud the kind of thing an adult once said to her. Eventually the speech moves inward, becoming the silent inner speech with which older children and adults plan and check their work. On this view the talk does not die out; it goes underground.

[4] The two accounts make different predictions, and Vygotsky set out to test them. If self-directed talk is merely a by-product of immature thinking, a harder task should not call forth more of it. If it is a tool for solving problems, it should increase when a child runs into one. Vygotsky and his colleagues placed small obstacles in children's activities (a pencil of the needed color missing when a child sat down to draw, for example) and reported that the amount of self-directed talk rose sharply, by their measure nearly doubling. A child who could not find a blue pencil might say, to no one, that the blue was gone, that red would have to do, and that a little water might make the red look dark enough.

[5] Vygotsky also reported a reverse experiment. If the talk was truly unconcerned with listeners, it should not matter who was in the room. But when children were placed among others who could not understand them, such as children who were deaf or who spoke another language, their self-directed talk dropped off. The speech was private in its aim but still social in its origins: the child, though talking to herself, behaved as if speaking were something one does among people who might understand.

[6] Later researchers, among them the American psychologist Laura Berk, took the question into ordinary classrooms. What is now usually called private speech turned out to be common well past the age at which Piaget expected it to vanish, though it changes form as children grow, shrinking from full sentences to fragments, then to whispers and silent movements of the lips. It tends to be most frequent when a task is challenging but manageable, and studies have generally found that children who use more task-relevant private speech go on to do better on those tasks than children who use less.

It is not the disappearance of a deficiency but the internalization of a skill, and a classroom rule that demands silent work may, for some young children, be asking them to give up the tool before they can use it without speaking.

[1] Ruth Ambler published "Stairwell Lantern" in a small quarterly in 1951, when she was twenty-six, and for the next forty years she would not leave it alone. The poem appears in every one of her six collections, and it is never quite the same poem twice. When her papers came to a university library after her death, they held, in addition to the six printed texts, five typescripts marked in her hand, the last dated three months before she died. Counting generously, there are eleven versions of a poem that is, in every one of them, fewer than twenty lines long.

[2] The early version is the one most readers know, because the 1951 text was reprinted in anthologies for decades and is the one teachers still photocopy. It is a poem of plain statement: a woman climbing the stairs of a tenement at night with a lantern, counting the doors, hearing behind each one a household she will never meet. Its last line, "and every door a lit room I was not in," is the line people quote, and it is easy to see why. It is a complaint, and a beautiful one.

[3] The later versions take the complaint apart. By the 1964 collection the woman has stopped counting the doors. By 1977 the last line has become "and every door a room, and I the light," which turns the speaker from someone shut out into the source of the light the other households see by. The final typescript goes further still and cuts the last line altogether, ending on the image of the lantern set down on the top step, still burning, while the speaker goes in. Read in sequence, the revisions move steadily away from the poem's original grievance toward something harder to name, a kind of contentment that the young poet would perhaps not have recognized and might not have trusted.

[4] For the editor of a collected edition, this sequence presents a choice with no comfortable answer. The long-standing rule of textual editing has been to print the author's final intention, on the reasoning that a writer's last word is her considered one. By that rule, the edition should print the final typescript, the one without the famous line, and relegate the 1951 poem to the notes. Many readers find that outcome close to vandalism. The young poet's line is the one that entered the language; to bury it in an appendix because its author later outgrew it seems to grant the old poet a power over the young one that no one would grant over another person.

[5] The opposing rule, which is to print the text as first published, the version that met the world, has problems of its own. It treats forty years of deliberate work as a kind of tampering. Ambler did not drift into her revisions. Her typescripts show her trying lines and striking them, restoring words she had cut a decade earlier, writing in the margin of the 1977 text, "closer, not there." Whatever else the revisions are, they are not the accidents of a careless old age.

[6] It may be that the question is badly put. Asking which version is "Stairwell Lantern" assumes that the poem is a single object of which the versions are better and worse copies. Ambler's papers suggest instead that the poem was, for her, the whole forty-year exchange: a young woman's complaint, answered over decades by the woman she became. Seen that way, the final typescript is not a correction of the 1951 text but a reply to it, and a reply makes no sense without the thing it answers.

[7] An edition built on that view would print the versions together, early to late, so that a reader meets the famous line and then watches it change. That is more cumbersome than a single clean text, and it will not please the anthologists. But it is the only arrangement in which nothing Ambler wrote is treated as a mistake, including, perhaps especially, the line she spent her life revising.

passage_title: Can a Fault Announce Itself? Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] For most of the past half century, the official position of seismology on earthquake prediction has been a polite refusal. No method has reliably told anyone the time, place, and size of a coming earthquake, and a long list of proposed signals, from odd animal behavior to changes in well water to radon gas in the soil, has failed to hold up under scrutiny. I share that history of disappointment. What I do not share is the conclusion often drawn from it: that large earthquakes arrive without any physical preparation that instruments could ever detect.

[2] The case for looking again comes from geodesy, the measurement of the ground's shape and motion, rather than from seismology proper. Japan now operates a network of more than a thousand continuously recording GPS stations, and similar networks have spread along other subduction zones, where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. These instruments can detect the ground moving by a few millimeters. They have shown that faults do not simply stick and then snap. Parts of a fault can creep forward over days or weeks, releasing strain without the violent shaking of an earthquake, a process known as slow slip.

[3] Before several large earthquakes, slow slip and swarms of small earthquakes appear to have migrated toward the eventual rupture zone. Before the magnitude 9.0 Tohoku earthquake of March 2011, a sequence of smaller shocks, including one of about magnitude 7.3 two days earlier, crept along the fault toward the point where the great rupture began. A similar pattern of foreshocks and slow slip preceded the magnitude 8.2 earthquake off Iquique, Chile, in 2014. These are not anecdotes about animals. They are measurements of the fault itself.

[4] I do not claim that these signals could have produced a warning. In both cases the pattern was recognized clearly only afterward. My claim is narrower: that a fault approaching failure may sometimes behave differently from one that is not, and that dense instruments can now, in principle, see the difference. Whether the difference is consistent enough to act on is a question that can be answered only by watching many more faults, in real time, before they break.

[1] For most of the past half century, the official position of seismology on earthquake prediction has been a polite refusal. Parts of a fault can creep forward over days or weeks, releasing strain without the violent shaking of an earthquake, a process known as slow slip.

[3] Before several large earthquakes, slow slip and swarms of small earthquakes appear to have migrated toward the eventual rupture zone. A similar pattern of foreshocks and slow slip preceded the magnitude 8.2 earthquake off Iquique, Chile, in 2014. These are not anecdotes about animals. They are measurements of the fault itself.

[4] I do not claim that these signals could have produced a warning. In both cases the pattern was recognized clearly only afterward. My claim is narrower: that a fault approaching failure may sometimes behave differently from one that is not, and that dense instruments can now, in principle, see the difference. Whether the difference is consistent enough to act on is a question that can be answered only by watching many more faults, in real time, before they break.
